Music Industry Shenanigans

By: Ntokozo Miya | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We take a peak into the dark side of the music industry - often perceived to be a world of glitz and glamour, it is a cutthroat space and many artists continue to fall victim to greedy opportunists.

Unique Selling Point:
Among others, we speak SA's biggest musicians, Zahara and Theuns Jordaan to illustrate that even successful stars are not immune to financial disputes with record labels. Also, both are doing well to get their careers back on track after setbacks stemming from legal battles with their former managers.

Summary:
Why do many South African musicians die poor? The biggest problem in the music industry is the non-existent and/or unread contract – the underlying issue with all our case studies. Without a contract or with a dubious contract, some record labels and artist managers are able to help themselves to a huge chunk of the artists' incomes – which explains why some of the country's biggest musician die broke despite being hugely successful in the public eye.

Further information:
We track the musical journey through the eyes of artists whose dreams were shattered by bad experiences with their various record labels. The issues range from contractual disputes as well as poor financial and career management. We also illustrate that it's not just musicians who are targeted by unscrupulous characters, even people in supporting roles including marketing managers and event planners are fair game.

MUSIC INDUSTRY SHENANIGANS – FOR MIX EDIT
 
AUDIO
VO – Designer clothes, flashy cars and exclusive parties – often perceived to be a world of glitz and glamour, the South African music industry is booming and according to a PwC study, raked in two point two billion rands from album sales and live music in 2016 – and yet, musicians say they are not cashing in as much as they deserve.
MKHUSELI 'KHUSTAR' NOMKALA – MUSICIAN
 
I didn't get paid for anything.
BULELWA 'ZAHARA' MKUTUKANA – MUSICIAN
 
I didn't know I had be paid or whatever.
THEUNS JORDAAN – MUSICIAN
 
I'm reluctant to create new content because I'm actually scared that I will be short-paid on it.
VO – They accuse record labels of using complicated contracts to pocket a large percentage of the money generated by the artists' music. Could this be why some artists end up broke, or worse, die in poverty?
LINK - Payment disputes are an age-old phenomenon in the music industry that not only affects the artists' pockets but their mental wellbeing as well, as they struggle to align their illustrious careers with empty bank accounts.
VO – Village girl turned superstar, Bulelwa 'Zahara' Mkutukana, moved to Johannesburg from the Eastern Cape in 2010, after she was spotted by TK Nciza, who co-owned TS Records with Sbusiso 'DJ Sbu' Leope. Zahara was accommodated and cared for by Nciza while she worked on her first album.
BULELWA 'ZAHARA' MKUTUKANA – MUSICIAN
 
I knew I had to be paid when I do my own album.
VO – Zahara knew little about the music industry and was happy to have her record label bosses take the lead on business decisions.
 
Her debut album Loliwe won her millions of fans and went on to win in six categories at the South African Music Awards in 2012.
BULELWA 'ZAHARA' MKUTUKANA – MUSICIAN
 
I always wanted to inspire people. I felt like people are being inspired.
VO - Even back then, Zahara says the royalties she received from her album sales were not music to her ears. She wants half of the proceeds but says the contract she signed gives her much less.
MASA - So the artists gets a very small fraction?
 
ZAHARA – Yo! You say 'small' but it's actually nothing. I write my own songs. I play that guitar. I do my own backing vocals...but I don't have 50/50 with them. So many of our artists, because of these things, they kill themselves. They take drugs. I find myself finishing a bottle of wine by myself.
VO – Intricate contracts are at the core of most disputes in the music industry, both locally and internationally.
 
Just last week, US rapper Kanye West and EMI Publishing settled out of court when the star fought to get out of the contract, which prohibited him from retiring as a songwriter and recording artist.
 
Earlier this year, Taylor Swift lost the rights to her music from the first six albums o her record label - that means anyone who wants to use the songs in adverts or movies will have to pay the label and not her.
 
It's widely reported that local rapper Fifi Cooper started her own record label after leaving her former stable following payment and contractual disputes.
 
Music business consultant Vusi Leeuw, who has worked with industry giants such as the late Hugh Masekela and major record labels including Universal Music, says artists shouldn't be too eager to put pen to paper.
VUSI LEEUW – MUSIC BUSINESS CONSULTANT
 
 
I think it's about people just wanting to grab the opportunity at whatever cost , worried that maybe the record label might change their minds and say we are not going to sign you.
VO – Once a contract is signed, it is assumed that the artist is satisfied with the terms, which at times, considerably favour the record label.
VUSI LEEUW – MUSIC BUSINESS CONSULTANT
 
You are developing an artist and there is a lot of investment financially – how do you protect yourself from a situation where you've developed this artist today and next thing, he's recording for another record label that has not spent anything.
VO - A sure way to avoid contractual conflict is to seek legal counsel before signing.
 
In a statement, TS Records wrote that both Zahara and her producer “were paid and continue to receive all forms of royalties that are due to them.” Zahara wants the conflict resolved out of court to avoid a legal showdown.
UPSOUND - Theuns performance
VO - Singer and songwriter Theuns Jordaan, says his record label, Coleske Artists, didn't disclose the full income from his album sales.
 
The two-time South African Music Award winner joined Coleske Artists on a verbal contract in 2009 and since then, received monthly statements detailing profits from his record sales. Jordaan says it was only in 2016 that he noticed an amount on the statement that the label had not paid to him.
THEUNS JORDAAN – MUSICIAN
 
There was a 10% in the turnover that was not disclosed. My statement, it starts with a number that says gross but we found out that that gross is a number minus 10%.
VO – Jordaan is suing Coleske Artists for a share of what he deems to be the “undisclosed amount.”
THEUNS JORDAAN – MUSICIAN
 
There is a summons for R2 million for Coleske that we believe they were hiding.
VO - Director at Coleske Artists, Brendon Hargroves, says the label plans to defend the summons in court, and that Jordaan has grossly misunderstood the statements, despite their efforts to clarify the contents to him.
BRANDON HARGROVES – COLESKE ARTISTS
 
We did not bank the money and I've showed you the documentation to that extent.Theuns' business manager was in the meeting and it was detailed and explained how he would earn between R20 and R24 a unit, nett out, and he understood it at that stage as did she.
VO – He explained that musicians at Coleske Artists are paid around a third of sixty-four rands, the price to retailer per CD, which is lower than the retail price at music stores. Less deductions including a retail discount and manufacturing costs, artists collect about twenty rands per CD sold.
 
According to the label, the ten per cent that Jordaan calls a 'hidden income' actually forms part of the retail price and is not paid to Coleske Artists. It is a handling fee paid to an independent company that facilitates music distribution to retailers.
LINK - While some artists have the resources to take on their record labels legally, others lose this David and Goliath battle before it even starts because they have no money to put up a fight.
VO – Cape Town-based musician Mkhuseli Nomkala, stage name Khustar, thought he'd hit the big time after getting a record deal through artist manager China Mpololo back in 2013. But behind the public show of success, Khustar was troubled. He'd lived with Mpololo in Joburg while doing work on his debut album Bubomi. Mpololo didn't pay him for his music but made sure he had groceries.
MKHUSELI 'KHUSTAR' NOMKALA – MUSICIAN
 
I wasn't used to being paid in groceries.Your music plays on the radio but you are sitting at home, without so much as R1. People think Khustar is living the good life, but I live in a shack. China just vanished.
VO – Khustar had no idea how he and his manager would split profits from Khustar's album sales and performances, but he signed the contract anyway.
MKHUSELI 'KHUSTAR' NOMKALA – MUSICIAN
 
I couldn't go through the contract because there's big words in the contract. I didn't understand it but I was hungry for this.
VO – Unable to afford a lawyer, Khustar is seeking legal advice from a law clinic about how he can claim some money from Mpololo.
 
The music industry is a cutthroat space and it's not just musicians who say they are being exploited, support personnel such as publicists and event managers say they're fair game too.
 
Over and above being an artist manager, Mpololo is the brain behind the SAAFMAs, South African Afro Music Awards.
 
Nono Matuwane says Mpololo hired her as a publicist for this year's awards ceremony but did not give her a contract.
NONO MATUWANE – PUBLICIST
 
I said to him I will do this work for you for R50k over 3 months. He owes me R15k because I only counted one month.
 
MASA – Why did you put so much energy and work when there was no contract?
 
NONO – I don't know what blinded me at that time because I came across articles that were talking about him owing people money or him claiming that people owe him.
VO – Nono has approached the small claims court with her demands for payment from Mpololo.
 
And so has Michelle Setuke, who Mpololo roped in as project manager for the awards. She also worked without a contract.
MICHELLE SETUKE – PROJECT MANAGER
 
I just wanted more and I felt that this would have given me more, and a bigger platform for my events company.
VO – She claims Mpololo owes her eighteen thousand rands.
MICHELLE SETUKE – PROJECT MANAGER
 
It's been difficult since then to get the money back.
VO – We sent numerous emails and made several calls to try and get Mpololo's side of the story but he didn't respond. We did eventually get through to his office, but still, we were no closer to getting answers.
UPSOUND
 
He is out of the country. That is the information I was told to give you.
LINK - Government has numerous initiatives to try and curb the exploitation of artists but do these efforts actually reach their intended audience?
VO - Zahara reached out to the department of sports, arts and culture, hoping to get intervention in the matter with her former record label.
BULELWA 'ZAHARA' MKUTUKANA – MUSICIAN
 
When there's elections, even when you are overseas, they call you back home but when we have problems, they don't care.
VO – Asanda Magaqa of the department says it's distressing to hear that artists feel neglected.
ASANDA MAGAQA – DEPARTMENT OF ARTS AND CULTURE
 
I would really encourage you to avail my contact details so that we immediately address the concern that she was ignored because it is not in the culture of the department to treat any stakeholder in that manner.
VO – The department says the Moshito Music Conference and Exhibition is just one of the many ways it tries to empower participants in the music business.
ASANDA MAGAQA – DEPARTMENT OF ARTS AND CULTURE
 
The music industry had limited access to credible business intelligence, it was then decided that Moshito be established to assist in informing and inspiring practitioners by giving them access to credible business intelligence.
VUSI LEEUW – MUSIC BUSINESS CONSULTANT
 
There's conferences almost every week, free information but artists don't attend.
VO – The musicians we spoke to say they've made changes to protect themselves in the future.
THEUNS JORDAAN – MUSICIAN
 
I'm checking my statements a lot better now.
VO – Khustar plans to rebuild his brand while Zahara now keeps the business in the family.
BULELWA 'ZAHARA' MKUTUKANA – MUSICIAN
 
My manager is Oyama, my cousin. I'm in a good place, but that doesn't mean I don't want money. I still want my money.
 
PROMOS
 
The country's biggest musicians say they should have been raking in the millions but disputes with their record labels mean they've had to settle for much less than they deserve.
 
Musicians and record labels fight it out over performance fees and royalties – experts say misunderstood contracts are at the core of most disputes in the music industry.
 
Glitzy and glamorous – South Africa’s multi-million rand music industry is booming but in this cutthroat space, are artists really getting their fair share of the profits?

Also, both are doing well to get their careers back on track after setbacks stemming from legal battles with their former managers.
metadata.Summary: Why do many South African musicians die poor? The biggest problem in the music industry is the non-existent and/or unread contract – the underlying issue with all our case studies. Without a contract or with a dubious contract, some record labels and artist managers are able to help themselves to a huge chunk of the artists' incomes – which explains why some of the country's biggest musician die broke despite being hugely successful in the public eye.
metadata.Further information: We track the musical journey through the eyes of artists whose dreams were shattered by bad experiences with their various record labels. The issues range from contractual disputes as well as poor financial and career management. We also illustrate that it's not just musicians who are targeted by unscrupulous characters, even people in supporting roles including marketing managers and event planners are fair game.
